<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. John W. Mannion, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 4986, the Parents Opt-in Protection Act,\1\ would amend the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment\2\ (PPRA) to require schools to obtain written consent from parents for each individual survey covering certain topics, as defined by law. Under the guise of parents' rights, the bill would make it more difficult for schools and districts to conduct student surveys, including mental health surveys. Further, it would replace the balanced approach to parents' rights and gathering data using surveys under current law with an opt-in requirement for which schools would need to obtain written consent from parents for each individual survey covering certain topics. This will make it harder for schools to collect critical information on student mental health, school climate, and safety. H.R. 4986 does this while offering no new rights for parents. The National Women's Law Center Action Fund\3\ and the Human Rights Campaign\4\ expressed opposition to the legislation.
\1\Parents Opt-in Protection Act, H.R. 4986, 119th Cong. (2025).
\2\20 U.S.C. Sec.  1232h. PPRA regulations are found at 34 C.F.R. Part 98.
\3\Letter from National Women's Law Center Action Fund to the Honorable Tim Walberg, Chair, and the Honorable Robert ``Bobby'' Scott, Ranking Member, H. Comm. on Educ. & Workforce, regarding H.R. 4986, the Parents Opt-in Protection Act (July 21, 2026) (on file with Committee Democratic staff).
\4\Letter from the Human Rights Campaign to Members of Congress regarding H.R. 4986, the Parents Opt-in Protection Act (July 20, 2026) (on file with Committee Democratic staff).
BACKGROUND
Parents' Rights and Student Privacy Safeguards Are Enshrined in Statute
The General Education Provisions Act\5\ (GEPA), originally enacted as part of the Elementary and Secondary Amendments of 1967, includes ``statutory provisions that are applicable to the majority of federal education programs administered by the U.S. Department of Education (ED), as well as provisions related to the powers and responsibilities of ED.''\6\ In 1974, amendments to GEPA added the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act\7\ (FERPA), which guarantees parents and guardians access to their minor student's education records and limits the disclosure of such records to outside entities, and the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment\8\ (PPRA), which provides parents the right to access instructional materials used in their student's curriculum as well as rights over the collection of their student's data.\9\
\5\20 U.S.C. Sec. Sec.  1221 et seq.
\6\Rebecca Skinner & Jody Feder, Cong. Rsch. Serv., R41119, General Education Provisions Act (GEPA): Overview and Issues (2010).
\7\Pub. L. No. 93-380, 88 Stat. 484 (codified as amended at 20 U.S.C. Sec.  1232g). FERPA regulations are found at 34 C.F.R. Part 99.
\8\Id. (codified as amended at 20 U.S.C. Sec.  1232h). PPRA regulations are found at 34 C.F.R. Part 98.
\9\Both FERPA and PPRA establish protections and provide rights over student data to parents and guardians of students under the age of 18; the protections and rights transfer directly to a student upon reaching the age of majority or attending a postsecondary institution. For the purposes of these Minority Views, we will refer to the protections and rights as belonging to parents (including guardians and emancipated and adult minors) in the context of K-12 education.
PPRA serves a number of important roles in protecting both parents' rights and student data. For example, PPRA provides parents the right to access instructional materials used in their student's curriculum.\10\ It also provides parents the right to access instructional materials that will be used as part of a survey, analysis, or evaluation\11\ as well as the right to inspect a survey itself.\12\ PPRA also recognizes eight sensitive topics that might be raised in questions that are part of a survey. The eight enumerated sensitive topics are:
\10\20 U.S.C. 1232h(c)(1)(C)(i). Additionally, Title I of ESEA requires that districts conduct outreach to parents and family members, and implement programs, activities, and procedures to involve parents and families in their child's education. 20 U.S.C. 6318(a)(1), (b),
(d); 20 U.S.C. 6311(d); 20 U.S.C. 6314(b). Under the law, each district that receives Title I funds must have a written parent and family engagement policy in place that, in part, provides parents with a description and explanation of the curriculum and assessments used in their child's school. 20 U.S.C. 6318(a)(1); 20 U.S.C. 6318(b), (d). Districts and schools must distribute this policy to parents and family members and hold at least one annual meeting with families to explain the policy and their right to be involved. 20 U.S.C. 6318.
\11\20 U.S.C. 1232(h)(a).

Rsch. Serv., General Education Provisions Act (GEPA): Overview and Issues (Mar. 18, 2010), https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/ 20100318_R41119_5a354cfda1d0c171d9b65ef88f95a 401330ab359.pdf.
The policies surrounding the administration of a survey involving any of these sensitive topics depend on whether the survey is given under a program administered by ED or whether it is not given as part of such a program but is nonetheless given by an LEA that receives federal funding. In either case, no student is ever required to take a survey that touches on one of these sensitive topics.
If a survey addresses one of the enumerated topics and is given as part of a program administered by ED, PPRA requires that parents provide prior written consent, which may be done as a single, annual consent for any such surveys; adult or emancipated students must also provide prior consent though it does not have to be in writing.\14\ If a survey is given not as part of a program administered by ED but by an LEA that receives federal funding from ED, PPRA requires that LEAs develop policies, in consultation with families, to protect student data privacy and govern the disclosure of student information.\15\ Further, PPRA identifies three types of activities for which parents: (1) must be given advance notice ``at least annually at the beginning of the school year,'' including ``specific or approximate dates'' when the activities are expected to occur;\16\ and (2) have the right to opt their child out of these activities.\17\ The activities include: instances in which their child's information may be used for marketing or sales; certain ``nonemergency, invasive physical examination[s] or screening[s]''; and any survey that addresses one or more of specifically enumerated topics.\18\

Thus, current law does not require students to participate in surveys that touch on these enumerated topics. But current law does require either written consent of a parent before a student may participate or parental notification with the option to opt out of such surveys. The GOP's Parental Rights Campaign
The discussion about the roles and rights of parents in their children's education has existed since the inception of formal education, and modern efforts in the U.S. are evidenced by the creation of the National Parent Teacher Association in 1897.\19\ Democrats agree that parental engagement is critical to student success. In 2024 the Biden-led U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention stated, ``Parental engagement in schools is closely linked to better student behavior, higher academic achievement, and enhanced social skills.''\20\ Moreover, the U.S. Supreme Court has declared ``the interest of parents in the care, custody, and control of their children is perhaps the oldest of the fundamental liberty interests recognized by this Court.''\21\
\19\National PTA, History, https://www.pta.org/home/About-National- Parent-Teacher-Association/ Mission-Values/National-PTA- History (last visited July 22, 2026).
\20\U.S. Ctrs. for Disease Control & Prevention, Parent Engagement in Schools (Nov. 22, 2024), https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-youth-parent-resources/parent-engagement/index.html#::text= Parent%20engagement%20is%20closely%20linked,as%20tobacco%20use%20or%20vi olence.

However, the recent parents' rights campaign--involving book bans, demanding control of curricula from a narrow and whitewashed perspective, and targeting transgender students, among other efforts--``has become a staple of some conservative attacks on public education.''\22\ Many have noted the ways this debate turns schools into political battlegrounds, separates communities, and diverts teachers' and children's attention away from teaching and learning.\23\ These efforts claim to provide parents with additional control over their students' education despite the fact that many of the rights being proposed already exist in state and federal law.\24\
